newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian government shaken one week into office.
newsitem.headline: Indian government shaken one week into office.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral faced his first shock waves in office on Monday as pressure built on the leader of his party to quit over a corruption case and leftwing allies denounced his budget.

Compounding Gujral's worries after a week in office was the possibility former finance minister P. Chidambaram's party would decide to remain out of the government, depriving the ruling United Front coalition of a key partner and economic strategist.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) said on Monday it had decided to prosecute Laloo Prasad Yadav, president of Gujral's Janata Dal party and chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, in a probe into the use of state funds.
But Yadav defiantly refused calls from some politicians that he should resign.
"Why should I resign?" he was quoted by the Press Trust of India as saying.
"I will go to the people's court for a verdict and fight the case in the court of law. I am fully confident that I will win."

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) said it had decided to prosecute Yadav and 55 others in a probe into the use of state animal welfare funds. The 10 billion rupee ($280 million) "animal fodder" scandal involved the alleged misuse of funds from the welfare scheme.
A CBI spokesman said junior Rural Areas and Employment Minister Chandradeo Prasad Varma would also be prosecuted. Yadav and Varma said they were innocent.
The federal police agency will request authorisation from Bihar governor A.R. Kidwai to indict Yadav, the spokesman said.
If the governor approves the move, the CBI will charge Yadav with violating the Prevention of Corruption Act, which carries a maximum penalty of seven years in jail, CBI officials said.

Four left-wing parties in Gujral's coalition called on Yadav and Varma to quit their government posts and face judicial proceedings. "This is necessary to conform to the norms of public conduct and propriety," they said in a joint statement.
Opposition leader Atal Bihari Vajpayee of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party concurred.
"The United Front government has a commitment to deal with corruption cases, and I can only hope that it would adopt the same attitude against the Bihar chief minister," he said.
Amar Singh, general secretary of the Samajwadi Party, also in the United Front, urged Yadav to quit as head of Janata Dal.

Gujral and his ousted predecessor, former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda, belong to the Janata Dal, which is the biggest component of the 15-party United Front coalition with 45 of its 178 deputies in the 545-seat lower house of parliament.
The Statesman newspaper said the decision to prosecute Yadav could "have far-reaching implications in Indian politics, which might even lead to the instability of the week-old Gujral government".
Adding to Gujral's woes was a call by four left-wing parties in his coalition for changes in the pathbreaking 1997/98 (April-March) budget, due to be taken up by parliament this week.
The Left Front issued a statement calling for changes in the areas of insurance, taxes, divestment in state enterprises, public distribution, customs duties and excise duties.
The budget, which would cut taxes and boost private investment, was seen as a litmus test of both the new government's commitment to economic reforms and its cohesion.

Gujral's government was also awaiting word from former finance minister P. Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) on whether the regional party would decide to join the government. Chidambaram was the main economic strategist in Deve Gowda's cabinet and drafted the budget.
TMC officials said party leader G.K. Moopanar might wait until the shock waves from the fodder scandal had dissipated before taking a decision on whether to join the government.
